samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The 2023 Orionid meteor shower, an annual event caused by debris from Halley's Comet, peaked on the morning of October 22, 2023. It is classified as a medium-strength shower, typically producing 10 to 20 meteors per hour in dark sky conditions. Some outlets reported a potential for up to 23 meteors per hour. The shower was active from early October through early November, with specific date ranges cited as October 2 to November 7. While peak activity was predicted for the evening of October 21, the best viewing was in the pre-dawn hours of October 22, when the radiant in the constellation Orion was highest in the sky and the first-quarter moon had set, creating favorable dark-sky conditions. <2> The Draconid meteor shower, an annual event, peaked on the evening of October 8, 2023, and remained active from October 6 to October 10. [2, 3] While typically a minor shower producing around 10 meteors per hour, the Draconids are notable for being best viewed in the early evening just after sunset, unlike most showers which are best seen after midnight. [2, 3] They are caused by debris from the periodic comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner. [2] The shower has a history of being unpredictable, with some years being very quiet while others, such as 1933 and 1946, produced spectacular meteor storms with thousands of meteors per hour. [4, 8] The 2023 event was anticipated to be favorable for viewing due to the moon being less than 20% illuminated, providing dark skies. [2] <3> The Perseid meteor shower, widely regarded as one of the most spectacular of the year, is an annual celestial event active from mid-July to late August. It is known for producing a high rate of bright meteors, often between 50 to 100 per hour under ideal conditions, and is also recognized for its fireballs—larger and more brilliant explosions of light and color. The shower appears to radiate from the constellation Perseus, which is how it gets its name. The parent comet responsible for the debris stream that creates the meteors is 109P/Swift-Tuttle. For the year 2023, the shower's peak activity was on the night of August 12th and the early morning hours of August 13th. Viewing is best in the Northern Hemisphere during the pre-dawn hours. <4> The Alpha Capricornid meteor shower is an annual event active from early July to mid-August, with sources specifying activity from approximately July 7th to August 15th. [5] While it is not a prolific shower, typically producing low rates of about 2 to 5 meteors per hour, it is notable for generating a high number of bright fireballs. [3, 7] The shower's peak occurs at the end of July, around July 30-31. [2, 6] It is classified as a reliable Class II minor shower and is equally visible from both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. [4, 8] <5> The June Bootid meteor shower was active from June 22nd to July 2nd, 2023, with its peak activity occurring on June 27th. This meteor shower is known for its variable and generally weak activity, typically producing only one or two meteors per hour. However, it has been known to have surprising outbursts, such as in 1998 when it reached a zenithal hourly rate of 100. The parent body of the June Bootids is the short-period comet 7P/Pons-Winnecke. The radiant point of the shower, from which the meteors appear to originate, is located in the constellation Boötes. In 2023, viewing conditions were favorable as the first quarter moon set early in the evening on the peak night, leaving dark skies for observation. <6> The 2023 Eta Aquariid meteor shower, which originates from the debris of Halley's Comet, peaked in the pre-dawn hours of May 5 and May 6, 2023. NASA predicted a potential outburst, suggesting rates could reach 120-160 meteors per hour under ideal conditions. However, the shower's peak coincided with a full moon on May 5, which significantly obscured the visibility of fainter meteors. The shower is known for its fast meteors, traveling at approximately 148,000 mph (66 km/s), and the potential for bright fireballs with persistent, glowing trains. Due to the radiant's location in the constellation Aquarius, viewing conditions were more favorable in the Southern Hemisphere, with expected rates of up to 30 meteors per hour, while Northern Hemisphere observers had a much shorter viewing window before dawn with projected rates of around 10-15 per hour. Reports varied on the exact peak night, with some sources citing the morning of May 5 and others May 6, reflecting a broad maximum that lasts for about a week. <7> The Lyrid meteor shower, recognized as one of the oldest known celestial events with observations dating back 2,700 years to 687 BC in China, peaked on the night of April 22nd into the early morning of April 23rd, 2023. Caused by debris from the long-period comet C/1861 G1 (Thatcher), the shower is active annually from mid to late April. Observers in 2023 could anticipate seeing between 10 to 20 fast, bright meteors per hour during the peak, a rate typical for the Lyrids. The shower is also known for occasionally producing fireballs and, in rare instances, outbursts of up to 100 meteors per hour, with the last significant outburst recorded in 1982. Viewing conditions in 2023 were highly favorable as the peak occurred shortly after a new moon on April 19, ensuring a dark, moonless sky for optimal viewing. <8> The Gamma Normids meteor shower, a minor shower primarily visible from the Southern Hemisphere, was active from late February to late March 2023, with its peak occurring around March 15. [2, 3, 6, 7] For observers in the Northern Hemisphere, viewing conditions were highly unfavorable. [2, 3] The shower's radiant point, located in the constellation Norma, rises only a few hours before dawn in mid-northern latitudes, remaining very low on the horizon. [2, 3] For instance, from Washington D.C. or Mountain View, California, the estimated visible meteor count was close to zero per hour. [3] Adding to the poor visibility, the 2023 peak coincided with the last quarter Moon, whose light further obscured the faint meteors. The shower is known for producing a low peak rate of about six meteors per hour even under ideal conditions. [2, 7] <9> The α-Centaurid meteor shower was active from late January to late February 2023, with peak activity occurring on February 8th. This annual meteor shower is best viewed from the Southern Hemisphere, as its radiant point in the constellation Centaurus does not rise above the horizon for most observers in the Northern Hemisphere. While generally not visible in the northern latitudes, some glimpses were possible for those in the extreme southern United States. The shower is considered minor, typically producing about one to six meteors per hour at its peak. <10> The first meteor shower of 2023, the Quadrantids, peaked during the night of January 3rd and the morning of January 4th. [1, 2, 5] Considered one of the best annual meteor showers, it is known for a short, intense peak of just a few hours and for producing bright fireball meteors. [1, 3, 5] Under ideal dark-sky conditions, observers in the Northern Hemisphere could anticipate seeing between 60 and 200 meteors per hour. [1, 3] However, viewing conditions for the 2023 event were significantly hampered by a bright, waxing gibbous moon, which was nearly full and expected to obscure all but the brightest meteors. [3, 6, 7] The Quadrantids originate from the asteroid 2003 EH1. [3, 4]

For 2025, the shower will be active from July 12 to August 23, with peak activity predicted around July 29-30. This shower's radiant point is in the constellation Aquarius. The meteors are generally faint, and viewing is best in the pre-dawn hours away from city lights. The shower is best viewed from the Southern Hemisphere where the radiant is higher in the sky, though it is also visible at lower rates in the Northern Hemisphere. The parent body of the meteor shower is suspected to be Comet 96P/Machholz. During its activity period, it overlaps with the Perseid meteor shower, which is generally more active.
